class: One decision written in several places, each checking some of the conditions
symptom: Whether the agent may read a one-time code from the owner's mail was decided three times: the code step of a form checked the owner's permission and a human check but not the site; the sign-in / account-setup step checked only the site; the password reset of an existing account checked neither the permission nor the human check, and pressed Forgot (spending one of a site's few reset requests) before finding out it could not read the code. Greenhouse's 'enter the code to confirm you're a human' was refused by one of them and would not have been by another.
site: Any employer site that emails a code (Workday reset, Greenhouse security code, R+L Carriers form)
root_cause: Each step that needed a code was written when it was needed and copied only the conditions its author had in mind. Nothing made the steps share the decision, so the rule the owner gave (only where mail reads are allowed, only on employer sites, never a code that proves a human) was true of some steps and not others, and a new condition (the per-account read limit) would have had to be added three times.
why_tests_missed: Each step's tests checked its own behaviour with the mail reader stubbed out, so no test asked the same question of every step, and none looked at whether a reset was requested before the code could be read.
fix: emailed_codes.why_not() holds the rule; passcode_from_gmail, which every reader of a code goes through, asks it before it opens the mail; the reset asks before it presses Forgot; the human-check wording lives only in emailed_codes.py; reads are counted per account for 24 hours in login_guard (six).
prevention: When the same yes/no question is asked in more than one module, give it one function and route every asker through the thing they all share (here the mail reader), then test each asker against the same table of cases with the real reader, not a stub.
